title: Find the second-largest element without sorting (track top two in one pass).
shortTitle: Find the Second-Largest Element Without Sorting

s1_definition.profdef: Finding the second-largest element without sorting is a single-pass algorithm that maintains two trackers, the largest seen so far and the second-largest seen so far. For each element you first check if it beats the largest, in which case the old largest becomes the second-largest and the element becomes the new largest; otherwise you check if it is between the two and update the second-largest. This runs in linear time with constant extra space, far cheaper than sorting, which is N log N.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to know the two highest transactions on Priya's account this month, specifically the runner-up, because the top transaction is often a known salary credit and the second-highest is the one the risk team actually scrutinises. Instead of ranking every transaction, a clerk walks the list once holding a gold medal and a silver medal. When a bigger amount appears, the current gold holder is demoted to silver and the newcomer takes gold. By the end, the silver medal shows the second-largest.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a gold and a silver tracker; a new champion pushes gold down to silver, otherwise it may just claim silver.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Finding the second-largest element without sorting is a single-pass algorithm that maintains two trackers, the largest seen so far and the second-largest seen so far. For each element you first check if it beats the largest, in which case the old largest becomes the second-largest and the element becomes the new largest; otherwise you check if it is between the two and update the second-largest. This runs in linear time with constant extra space, far cheaper than sorting, which is N log N.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants to know the two highest transactions on Priya's account this month, specifically the runner-up, because the top transaction is often a known salary credit and the second-highest is the one the risk team actually scrutinises. Instead of ranking every transaction, a clerk walks the list once holding a gold medal and a silver medal. When a bigger amount appears, the current gold holder is demoted to silver and the newcomer takes gold. By the end, the silver medal shows the second-largest.

**One line to remember:** Keep a gold and a silver tracker; a new champion pushes gold down to silver, otherwise it may just claim silver.

sections.s2_technical:
You maintain two variables, largest and secondLargest, both conceptually starting at negative infinity, which in Java you represent with the smallest possible value for the type or, more safely, with a sentinel and a found flag. For each element you apply an ordered check. First, if the element is greater than largest, then the current largest is no longer the top, so you move largest into secondLargest and then set largest to the element. Otherwise, if the element is greater than secondLargest but strictly less than largest, you set secondLargest to the element.

The order of those two checks is critical. You must update secondLargest from the old largest before you overwrite largest, otherwise you lose the value that should become the runner-up. Getting that ordering wrong is the most common bug in this problem.

A key design decision is how to treat duplicates. If the largest value appears twice, is the second-largest the same value or the next distinct value? The requirement decides. For a strict distinct second-largest you add the condition that the element must be strictly less than largest to be a secondLargest candidate, which skips duplicates of the maximum. For a positional second-largest you allow equality. In banking I usually want the distinct second-highest amount, so I use the strict version.

A senior point is edge cases. An array with fewer than two elements has no second-largest, so I guard that and signal it clearly rather than returning a meaningless sentinel. An array where every element is identical also has no distinct second-largest under the strict definition, which I handle explicitly. Being precise about these cases is what separates a robust solution from one that passes only the happy path.

Another senior point is the data type and comparison. For money I use BigDecimal and compareTo for the reasons described earlier, and I avoid initialising the trackers with a magic minimum constant; instead I seed from the first two elements after sorting just those two, or I carry a found flag, which keeps the logic correct for negative amounts.

A small finance-domain example: `BigDecimal largest = a, secondLargest = b-or-less; for each x: if (x.compareTo(largest) > 0) { secondLargest = largest; largest = x; } else if (x.compareTo(largest) < 0 && x.compareTo(secondLargest) > 0) { secondLargest = x; }` yields the distinct runner-up in one pass.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India risk team monitors Priya's current account and wants the second-highest transaction of the month. The highest is usually a predictable large credit like a property rental settlement, so it is the runner-up that signals an unusual pattern worth reviewing. Finding the second-largest in a single pass, without sorting the whole month, is exactly this top-two tracking.

This is exactly how the second-largest scan works in Java — we hold a gold and a silver tracker and demote gold to silver whenever a bigger amount arrives.

Problem 2 — The month may contain duplicate large amounts, for example two identical rent credits, and the risk team wants the second-largest distinct amount, not a repeat of the maximum. So the code must use the strict version that skips duplicates of the largest, and it must handle a month with fewer than two distinct amounts by reporting that there is no runner-up.

What the code will do: a `RunnerUpService` class with `secondLargest(BigDecimal[] amounts)` that tracks the top two distinct values in one pass and guards the too-few-elements and all-equal cases. The demo scans Priya's monthly amounts including a duplicate and logs the distinct runner-up.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Priya's amounts are `250000`, `48000`, `250000`, `120000`, and `9000`.

Step 1: We guard the length; five elements is enough. Both largest and secondLargest start as null.

Step 2: First element `250000`. largest is null, so we demote null into secondLargest and set largest to `250000`. Now largest is `250000`, secondLargest is null.

Step 3: Element `48000`. It is not greater than `250000`. It is strictly less than largest and secondLargest is null, so secondLargest becomes `48000`.

Step 4: Element `250000` again. It is not greater than largest, because it equals it. The strict less-than check fails because it is not strictly below largest, so it is skipped. This is how duplicates of the maximum are ignored.

Step 5: Element `120000`. It is not greater than largest. It is strictly less than `250000` and greater than the current secondLargest `48000`, so secondLargest becomes `120000`.

Step 6: Element `9000`. It is not greater than largest and not greater than secondLargest `120000`, so nothing changes. The loop ends with largest `250000` and secondLargest `120000`. The distinct runner-up is `120000`, correctly skipping the duplicated maximum.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T15:50:00Z INFO Second-largest (distinct) = Rs.120000
2026-10-26T15:50:00Z INFO Risk review: second-highest distinct = Rs.120000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [250000, 48000, 250000, 120000, 9000]
    │
    ▼
  gold=null, silver=null
    │ 250000 → gold=250000
    │ 48000  → silver=48000
    │ 250000 → ==gold → SKIP (duplicate of max)
    │ 120000 → <gold, >silver → silver=120000
    │ 9000   → no change
    ▼
  gold=250000, silver=120000
    │
    ▼
  Output: distinct runner-up Rs.120000 (max duplicate ignored)
```
sections.s5d_lld:

```
  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Single-pass top-K (K=2) tracking                             │
  │  Optional return: models "no runner-up" without null/sentinel │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: RunnerUpService only computes the second-largest          │
  │  O: generalise to top-K with a small heap, callers unchanged  │
  │  D: callers depend on Optional<BigDecimal>, not the loop       │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │            RunnerUpService            │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + secondLargest(BigDecimal[])         │  Optional<BigDecimal>, O(n)
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
      secondLargest contract:
        Pre:  amounts may be null/short (returns empty)
        Post: distinct 2nd-largest, or empty if none exists
        Order rule: demote gold→silver BEFORE overwriting gold

  ── State Diagram: Element Handling ───────────────────────

  [x > gold] ──→ [silver = gold; gold = x]
  [x < gold && x > silver] ──→ [silver = x]
  [x == gold] ──→ [SKIP (distinct rule)]

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. RunnerUpDemo.main()
  2.   → secondLargest([250000,48000,250000,120000,9000])
  3.     → gold=250000, skip duplicate, silver=120000
  4.     → Optional.of(120000)
  5.   → log distinct runner-up
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the second-largest element without sorting is a single pass that tracks the top two values. I keep a largest and a second-largest, and for each element I apply an ordered check: if the element beats the largest, I first move the current largest down into the second-largest and then make the element the new largest; otherwise, if it sits strictly between the two, I update the second-largest. One pass gives the answer in linear time, which is cheaper than sorting.

The detail that trips most people up is the ordering inside the first branch. I must copy the old largest into the second-largest before I overwrite the largest, otherwise I lose the value that should become the runner-up. I also decide deliberately how to treat duplicates: for a distinct second-largest I require the candidate to be strictly less than the largest, which skips repeats of the maximum, and that is usually what the business wants.

I handle the edge cases explicitly. An array with fewer than two elements has no runner-up, and an array where everything equals the maximum has no distinct runner-up, so I return an Optional that is empty rather than a misleading sentinel. For money I use BigDecimal with compareTo and avoid magic minimum constants so negative amounts work correctly.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on the risk team's monthly scan of Priya's account, where the highest transaction is usually a predictable large credit like a rental settlement, so it is the second-highest distinct amount that actually gets scrutinised. The month often contains duplicate large amounts, so the strict distinct version correctly ignores the repeated maximum and reports the real runner-up. Explaining the ordering rule, the duplicate policy, and the Optional for the empty cases shows the interviewer that I handle the tricky parts, not just the obvious scan.
